description: We are from New Castelar College. We are a team of six students with complementary skills in software development, data analysis, and biological sciences. Our programmers focus on processing satellite data, developing analytical tools, and visualizing environmental trends, while our biologists contribute knowledge of plant health, soil conditions, and agricultural ecosystems. Our mission is to connect the power of space technology with the needs of agriculture on Earth.
summary:
Green Resilience: From Space to Soil is a free web app that tells farmers around San Pedro del Pinatar (Murcia, Spain) what to grow, where and when, both today and in a warmer, drier climate.

It combines NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture (2023–2025) with daily data from local SiAR weather stations, ISRIC SoilGrids soil maps and crop requirements from FAO and our team's biologists. For 10 crops and three zones (Coast, Town, Inland farmland), our model scores temperature, irrigation water and soil salinity, finds the best planting week and estimates how many cubic metres of water per hectare each crop needs.

The Field Shift lens lets users add up to +4 °C and cut rain by up to 40% to see how each crop's score, planting date and water need change.

The challenge asks how farming must shift as the climate changes. Our answer is a practical local tool: on an interactive map, a farmer picks a zone or a season and gets a ranked list of crops, with a plain-language explanation behind every number, in English and Spanish.
details:
Green Resilience tells a farmer in San Pedro del Pinatar what to plant, when, and how much water it will cost, and shows how warming and drought change the answer.

WHAT IT DOES

Green Resilience is an interactive map of San Pedro del Pinatar and its surroundings, split into three zones: Coast, Town and Inland farmland. A farmer picks a crop and a zone and sees:

- a crop suitability score (0–100%) and a plain verdict: good choice, possible with care, or not recommended;

- the best planting date and the expected harvest;

- how much irrigation water the crop needs (m³ per hectare);

- the main limiting factor, explained in one sentence ("Main limit: soil salinity, yield drops by 36% at this soil salinity").

Clicking a season (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter) shows a ranked catalogue of the best crops to plant in that season in the chosen zone. Every number has a "?" card that explains how it was calculated and which data it came from.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data. NASA SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP v008, the 9 km cell over San Pedro del Pinatar, 2023–2025) supplies daily root-zone soil moisture, which we use to estimate how much water is already stored in the soil at planting. Daily weather (temperature, rain, effective rain and reference evapotranspiration ET₀) comes from three local SiAR weather stations (Spanish Ministry of Agriculture) for the same years. ISRIC SoilGrids supplies soil texture and pH for each zone. Crop requirements (temperature range, water need, salt tolerance, planting months) come from our team's biologists, FAO-56 and FAO-61.

2. Cross-check of NASA and station data. We compared SMAP L4 weather with the three stations on 950–1,064 measured days. Daily mean temperature agrees very well (r = 0.98–0.99, SMAP 0.3–0.6 °C warmer), but the 9 km cell smooths extremes: nights about 4 °C warmer and days about 3 °C cooler than at the stations. Monthly rain correlates at r = 0.56–0.90, but SMAP gives 1.3–2 times more rain per year and about twice as many rainy days. Frost, heat stress and irrigation depend on exactly these extremes and rain totals, so we use the stations for weather and NASA SMAP for soil moisture, the variable that stations do not measure.

3. Model. For every crop, zone and planting week, and separately for each of the three years:

- Temperature: share of days inside the crop's ideal range, with penalties for frost and extreme heat; the length of the growing season follows accumulated growing degree days.

- Water: FAO-56 crop water use (Kc × ET₀) minus effective rain minus the water already stored in the soil at planting (NASA SMAP soil moisture with SoilGrids field capacity) gives the irrigation needed.

- Salinity: Maas–Hoffman yield loss at the zone's soil salinity. Sea asparagus (Salicornia) only scores well on the coast, where it can be irrigated with saline water.

- Soil pH: a soft penalty outside the crop's preferred range.

The final score is the geometric mean of temperature, water and salinity, multiplied by the pH factor, then averaged over 2023–2025.

4. Field Shift. The lens raises temperature by 0–4 °C (reference evaporation rises by about 3% per °C) and cuts rain to as low as 60% of today's. Every result is recomputed, so users see which crops win or lose and how planting dates move.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Murcia is one of the driest regions of mainland Spain and a major fruit and vegetable producer in Europe, and water is its scarcest resource. Our tool turns satellite and station data into decisions a farmer can act on: what to plant, when to plant it and how much water it will cost. Because it shows the impact of warming and drought crop by crop, it also helps farmers, cooperatives and local authorities plan the shift to more resilient crops before losses happen.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy) for data processing and the model; Streamlit for hosting; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface; MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap / OpenStreetMap vector tiles and Sentinel-2 cloudless satellite imagery for the map; GitHub for version control. The model is checked by 17 automated tests.

AI use: Claude Code (Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5) helped write and test the code; Claude (chat, [MODEL]) helped with data research, documentation and checking our assumptions. All data sources, crop parameters and model decisions were reviewed by the team.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a technical dashboard, we built a farmer-first map: simple verdicts and water in m³/ha instead of raw indices, a season catalogue, the Field Shift lens for climate scenarios, and a "?" explanation behind every number so nothing is a black box. The app is fully bilingual (English and Spanish) and works on phones.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Local salinity (a key problem in Campo de Cartagena), water scarcity and irrigation costs, frost and heat extremes, soil water at planting, year-to-year weather variability (three years averaged), and usability for non-technical users.

Limitations: scores are suitability indices, not yield forecasts, and are not yet calibrated against field yields. Zone borders and soil salinity values are approximate estimates. SMAP covers one 9 km cell. Seawater irrigation on the coast is assumed to be available. The +3% evaporation per °C is an assumed value. Some crop parameters are literature estimates still being reviewed by our biologists.
